transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2026-05-19 16:00 PT
Duration: ~72 minutes
Location: Zoom (recording)
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE); Priya Patel (Redwood SE); Marta Ruiz (Verdant Head of Security); Kenji Sato (Verdant Infra); Lina Zhang (Verdant Compliance); Ethan Brooks (Verdant Platform)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be rough):
- Goal: walk Verdant through proposed private deployment architecture for an air-gapped-ish enclave with a controlled egress proxy, KMS integration with HSM, and RBAC mapping to SSO groups.
- Main asks: SOC2 evidence, data residency constraints (EU region only), audit log retention to SIEM, key custody model, and hardened bastion/egress patterns.
- Agreed next steps: Redwood to share detailed diagram and egress playbook; run perf test; customer to share SOC2 contact and CIDRs.

Topics:
- Network isolation and segmentation
- Egress proxy / outbound firewalling patterns
- Bastion / jump host designs and ephemeral access
- KMS/HSM key custody and rotation policy integration
- RBAC mapping and SSO (Okta/SAML) sync
- Audit logs, retention, and SIEM integration
- Data residency and encryption at rest/in transit

Transcript body:
[00:00] Jordan Lee: all right hello everyone thanks for joining today, I'm Jordan from Redwood, i'm the AE on this account, and with me is Priya our solutions engineer. how's everyone doing?
[00:07] Marta Ruiz: good thanks Jordan. we are excited to get into the nitty gritty— we have some pretty strict constraints and Lina will talk about compliance.
[00:12] Priya Patel: hey hi team, i'll mostly drive the architecture and any perf/security details, feel free to interrupt — this is supposed to be a workshop.
[00:18] Kenji Sato: Kenji here, i'll have the network details and we can talk about peering, private links, that sort of thing.
[00:22] Lina Zhang: Lina — compliance, SOC2 + EU data residency questions.
[00:25] Ethan Brooks: Ethan, platform, i'll own the ops side and key rotation.

[00:30] Jordan Lee: quick agenda — we sketched a reference design for a "sealed enclave" or airgap-adjacent private deployment: private control plane, model serving in a private VPC, egress-only through a hardened proxy that we can route to a customer-managed egress gateway or to a restricted external service endpoint. we'll talk KMS/HSM options, RBAC mapping to Okta groups, and audit logs. then wrap with action items. any additions?
[00:46] Marta Ruiz: sounds right — one thing: we need to make sure the design avoids any uncontrolled DNS/metadata access. last time we saw a leak via instance metadata in a test.
[00:54] Priya Patel: noted, we have a pattern that explicitly disables IMDS access on the serving instances and routes any required secrets access through a private KMS endpoint. also mutual TLS to the egress proxy — so no cleartext.

[01:10] Kenji Sato: can you sketch how traffic flows again? we have no outbound internet allowed except through a proxy owned by us.
[01:18] Priya Patel: sure, high level: client requests hit customer's frontend, they forward inference requests to Redwood's private control plane (option A: customer-hosted control plane in their VPC, option B: Redwood-managed private control plane inside a customer VPC peered via AWS Transit Gateway). For serving, model workers run in the same private VPC; they have no default route to the internet, only an egress route through an internal egress proxy — which is a set of hardened EC2/NAT devices or a containerized proxy that performs TLS termination and outbound filtration.
[01:46] Priya Patel: important detail: KV cache and prefix caching stays local; no shared public caches. anything that must go to external telemetry is pushed to a customer SIEM via a secure forwarder (syslog over TLS).

[02:05] Lina Zhang: for SOC2, we need proof of auditability — can audit logs be forwarded to our SIEM with immutable storage and retention 7 years? that's long.
[02:14] Jordan Lee: we can forward logs to your SIEM; retention is then controlled on your end. Redwood can also provide signed audit bundles and we can support write-once object store for evidence archives for the pilot. we'd want to confirm retention policy and egress frequency — large volumes might need batching.

[02:40] Ethan Brooks: on KMS: we use a split custody model today with AWS KMS and a hardware security module for key wrapping, we cannot have plaintext keys in any 3rd-party service. how would Redwood integrate?
[02:50] Priya Patel: two supported patterns: 1) customer-managed KMS: Redwood's serving instances call your private KMS endpoint (VPC endpoint) and never persist plaintext. 2) Redwood-managed KMS with BYOK — keys are imported and wrapped by your HSM; Redwood stores only wrapped keys and uses HSM-backed unwrap calls via a private connection. for higher assurance, we recommend the customer-managed KMS + HSM approach.
[03:19] Kenji Sato: does that require egress to AWS KMS? we want no egress to public side.
[03:24] Priya Patel: no, KMS calls remain inside the VPC via interface endpoint, so no public egress. if you run an on-prem HSM, we can do a private peering/VPN for KMS operations.

[03:40] Marta Ruiz: what about rotation windows? our policy is 90 days for wrapping keys and monthly for key-use audit snapshots. can Redwood integrate hooks?
[03:48] Priya Patel: yes, we can call your KMS rotation API and generate rotation events in audit logs. we also emit key-use events to the audit stream that you can consume. note sometimes event names are mangled in transcriptions but we'll provide a mapping.

[04:05] Jordan Lee: quick interruption — competitor question: some teams consider "internal hosting" to avoid any data touching cloud vendors, are you weighing that option?
[04:12] Marta Ruiz: we are exploring it but it's heavy — our preference is a vendor that supports an airgapped or private VPC model with strict controls.

[04:22] Priya Patel: another important pattern: egress allowlist. We recommend an egress-proxy that enforces a tiny allowlist of destinations (for telemetry and for external model artifacts if needed) and does deep TLS inspection with mutual TLS back to those endpoints. This gives you an auditable choke point.

[04:43] Kenji Sato: deep TLS inspection — that can be sticky for cert pinning. do you support mutual TLS with cert rotation?
[04:49] Priya Patel: yes, the proxy supports mTLS; we can integrate with your cert manager (e.g., HashiCorp Vault PKI or your internal CA). certificate rotation is automated via a short-lived cert workflow.

[05:05] Lina Zhang: SSO and RBAC — we use Okta and map groups to roles. can we have Redwood map Okta groups to serving roles (read-only, model-admin, ops)? and enforce RBAC for API keys?
[05:15] Priya Patel: absolutely. Redwood supports SAML/OIDC federation; we can map Okta groups to RBAC roles. The control plane issues short-lived credentials for the serving runtime and we support scoping roles so that a model-admin cannot list customer secrets, etc. We also support token revocation via an SSO session revoke hook.

[05:39] Ethan Brooks: what about long-lived API keys we sometimes need for CI? we prefer short-lived but CI is a pain.
[05:45] Jordan Lee: pattern: issue short-lived tokens to a CI proxy running in your environment that exchanges a machine identity for a short token. we can help design that.

[05:58] Marta Ruiz: can you walk through a failure scenario — if the egress proxy is compromised what are the compensating controls?
[06:04] Priya Patel: good question. design-wise: 1) no plaintext secrets on disk; 2) KMS calls required for decryption and go through VPC endpoints; 3) network policy enforces only the proxy can reach outbound and the proxy has an allowlist; 4) HSM-backed key operations require dual auth if you opt for split custody; 5) audit logs are streamed off-proxy to your SIEM in near real-time, so detection is quick. for extreme cases we can configure automatic circuit-breakers that shut down egress if anomalous patterns detected.

[06:42] Kenji Sato: what's the expected telemetry volume for audit logs? we need sizing for SIEM ingest costs.
[06:48] Priya Patel: ballpark: per 1k requests with full token-level tracing it's ~50-150MB/day depending on prompting patterns. for pilot we'll instrument and provide an estimate.

[07:04] Marta Ruiz: data residency — we need EU-only for model input and embeddings. can Redwood guarantee no cross-region replication?
[07:12] Jordan Lee: yes, in Private deployments you can pin region and disable cross-region backups. snapshots can be stored to your customer-controlled bucket in region. we will include SLA language for region restrictions in the private contract.

[07:27] Lina Zhang: about audit evidence: SOC2 asks for capability to produce tamper-evident logs. does Redwood sign the logs?
[07:34] Priya Patel: we can produce signed audit bundles (GPG or PGP) and we support write-once object store for the bundles. we can also provide timeline correlation between user actions and model outputs for a given request id.

[07:55] Ethan Brooks: regarding firewalling, do you expect us to run Azure/AWS native firewall or do you support a managed firewall appliance?
[08:02] Priya Patel: we are flexible. Many customers use managed firewall appliances (Palo Alto NGFW, Fortinet) or cloud-native firewalls plus the egress proxy. we provide the ruleset and the minimum required ports/hosts. for on-prem you can route through an appliance in a DMZ with strict NAT.

[08:22] Jordan Lee: quick pause — can we get a show of hands on the key risk areas you want prioritized for the pilot? Marta?
[08:28] Marta Ruiz: KMS key custody and evidence for SOC2.
[08:31] Lina Zhang: RBAC mapping and audit log immutability.
[08:34] Kenji Sato: network CIDRs, peering, and egress proxy hardening.
[08:37] Ethan Brooks: perf and operational runbooks — how do we roll upgrades without impacting latency?

[08:44] Priya Patel: upgrade pattern: blue/green for model worker pools and canary for control plane changes. we recommend a canary window with tracing to detect regression; automatic rollback on error budgets. we'll share our runbook.

[09:00] Marta Ruiz: can we see a concrete example of the egress proxy policy? like what exact headers are removed, what is inspected, how tokens are redacted?
[09:10] Priya Patel: yes, example policy: remove Instance Metadata headers, strip any customer auth headers, redact tokens in payloads using regex patterns, mTLS to allowed destinations only, and block DNS over HTTPS unless allowed. we'll share sample policies.

[09:30] Kenji Sato: what about zero-trust microsegmentation inside the VPC?
[09:35] Priya Patel: recommend CNI + network policies; each model worker runs in its own nodepool with strict pod/network policies. we can integrate with your identity provider for pod identity and apply least privilege network flows.

[09:52] Jordan Lee: okay let's go through the proposed pilot scope — Priya, read the bullets.
[09:57] Priya Patel: 1) deploy Redwood Private control plane in a customer-managed VPC in eu-west-1; 2) provision model serving pool with no public egress, egress through customer egress proxy; 3) integrate with customer KMS endpoint (VPC interface) and HSM for wrap/unwrap; 4) map Okta groups to RBAC roles and demonstrate token revocation; 5) stream audit logs to customer SIEM with retention and signed bundles; 6) run a perf test replicating 10k tokens and provide latency/cost report.

[10:39] Lina Zhang: for SOC2 we'll need to see the service org control docs — can you share SOC2 Type II report and any ISO27001 certs?
[10:46] Jordan Lee: yes we'll provide SOC2 Type II and our compliance pack. note: for Private customers the scope is slightly different but we'll provide attestation for the Redwood-hosted components we manage.

[10:58] Ethan Brooks: about the signed bundles, how are they timestamped?
[11:02] Priya Patel: we embed an RFC-3339 timestamp and sign the bundle with a rotating signing key; we also include an index file that maps request IDs to log offsets.

[11:18] Kenji Sato: we run some workloads with short context windows — what are the options for KV cache persistence? we want that local only.
[11:25] Priya Patel: KV cache is local to the serving node and optionally backed by a customer-controlled redis inside the VPC. caching never goes to public caches unless explicitly configured.

[11:38] Jordan Lee: do you have questions about the SLA/uptime given this architecture?
[11:42] Marta Ruiz: yes, what is the SLA for private deployments and for incident response?
[11:47] Jordan Lee: Dedicated/private customers get a 99.9% uptime SLA for serving, with designated incident response contacts and a 1-hour P1 response for security incidents. we'll include SOC2-era runbooks in the contract.

[12:02] Lina Zhang: about pen testing — will Redwood allow us to run pen tests on the private deployment?
[12:08] Priya Patel: yes, with a coordinated testing window; we sign an engagement agreement and require an agreed blast radius. we can also provide pen test checklists.

[12:18] Ethan Brooks: logging format — do you provide structured JSON logs with schema? our SIEM prefers structured logs.
[12:24] Priya Patel: yes by default logs are JSON-LD structured; we can map fields to your SIEM schema and provide a sample ingestion pipeline.

[12:37] Kenji Sato: what about emergency access — breakout keys for on-call? we have an emergency access policy that requires a dual-approval workflow.
[12:44] Jordan Lee: we support short-lived emergency keys that require two orchestrated approvals; plus full audit trails.

[12:52] Marta Ruiz: are there any gotchas around model updates and storing model artifacts? we must ensure model artifacts are scanned and stored in-region only.
[12:59] Priya Patel: artifacts are stored in your region and can be scanned by your malware scanner (we provide hooks). if you prefer, you can host model artifacts in your own object store, and Redwood will pull them via internal network only.

[13:14] Lina Zhang: for the compliance pack, can we get an inventory of which controls map to SOC2 categories?
[13:19] Jordan Lee: yes, we'll map controls to common frameworks (SOC2/ISO/PCI) and provide the mapping doc.

[13:28] Kenji Sato: DNS handling — we run an internal recursive DNS, can the pods use internal DNS only?
[13:33] Priya Patel: yes, recommend using private DNS and a DNS firewall. we'll disable external resolvers on nodes.

[13:43] Ethan Brooks: one last operational question: how do we patch the serving nodes without impacting running requests?
[13:48] Priya Patel: rolling patch windows with connection draining; we also snapshot model states if needed. for stateful caches we prefer blue/green approaches.

[14:00] Marta Ruiz: thanks — this was useful. quick recap from our side: we want the architecture diagram, egress policy example, KMS integration guide, SOC2 docs, and perf test plan.
[14:12] Jordan Lee: great — we'll deliver those. any final questions?
[14:17] Lina Zhang: timeline — how soon can we kick off the pilot?
[14:20] Priya Patel: we can start provisioning in about 2 weeks pending order. pilot duration typically 4–6 weeks.

[14:30] Jordan Lee: okay we'll send the materials and book a follow-up next Tuesday to review the architecture diagram. thanks everyone.
[14:36] Marta Ruiz: thank you.
[14:38] Ethan Brooks: thanks all.

[14:40] End of recording.

Notes on transcription: occasional word substitutions and timestamps are nominal (every few minutes) — some speaker labels may be generic in the automated export. The conversation contained typical sales/back-and-forth and technical troubleshooting, with natural interruptions and clarifications.
